Intervals of enhanced nesting activity and hemispheric asymmetry broadly coincide with enhanced hemispheric quasi-biennial variability and temporal evolution of the large-scale solar magnetic field, suggesting a possible connection between intermediate-timescale dynamo variability and the hemispheric organization of solar activity.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes NOAA active regions during Solar Cycles 22-24 and finds significant North-South asymmetry in AR emergence, concentrated specifically in ARs participating in activity nests. Monte Carlo tests show 6-18% of ARs belong to a non-random, hemispherically asymmetric nesting component, linked to temporally offset bursts and reduced cross-equatorial coherence, suggesting a connection to intermediate-timescale dynamo variability.
AI.motivation: To investigate the distribution of active regions across solar longitude and time to understand whether North-South hemispheric asymmetry in AR emergence is a real statistical phenomenon and what physical mechanism (e.g., dynamo variability) drives it.
AI.method: Use of an activity-nest identification algorithm on NOAA AR data from Solar Cycles 22-24, combined with Monte Carlo tests using randomized longitudes and temporal perturbations to assess whether the observed nesting and asymmetry exceed random expectations.
AI.result: Nest-member ARs show substantially larger hemispheric asymmetry than the full or non-nest populations; ~6-18% of ARs participate in a non-random, asymmetric nesting component; asymmetry is associated with temporally offset bursts and distinct longitudinal clustering, reducing cross-equatorial coherence; nesting intervals coincide with enhanced hemispheric quasi-biennial variability.
AI.conclusion: The hemispheric asymmetry in solar AR emergence is real and primarily driven by activity-nest members, with nesting activity tied to intermediate-timescale dynamo variability and the evolution of the large-scale solar magnetic field, suggesting a physical link between dynamo processes and hemispheric organization of solar activity.

title: The Delay Time Distribution of Quasi-Periodic Eruptions
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, accepted to ApJL
summary: Quasi-periodic eruptions (QPEs) are quasi-periodic X-ray bursts observed in the nucleus of a galaxy. Multiple pieces of observational evidence link QPEs to tidal disruption events (TDEs), which occur when stars are disrupted after approaching a supermassive black hole too closely. Post-starburst galaxies are overrepresented among the host galaxies of both TDEs and QPEs, though the mechanism causing this overrepresentation is unknown. While their physical origin is unclear, the delay time distribution (DTD) of QPEs, or rate of QPEs as a function of time since a burst of star formation, can constrain what mechanisms influence the QPE rate and possible QPE formation channels. We compile a catalog of 10 QPE host galaxies with optical spectra, model the stellar populations with Bagpipes, and retrieve the age of the most recent burst of star formation to construct the DTD of QPEs. We find that the QPE rate increases with post-burst age to reach a peak at ~1 Gyr relative to a control sample, similar to the observational TDE DTD, though we cannot rule out a flat distribution of burst ages relative to a control sample. However, the fraction of QPE host galaxies with high (>1%) burst mass fractions is larger than the fraction of galaxies with high burst mass fractions in either a sample of TDE host galaxies or a sample of control galaxies. If the preferred QPE formation channel requires extreme mass ratio inspirals (EMRIs), then such EMRIs may be more readily produced by large, ~1-Gyr-old bursts of star formation.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs the delay time distribution (DTD) of quasi-periodic eruptions (QPEs) using a catalog of 10 QPE host galaxies, modeling their stellar populations with Bagpipes. The QPE rate peaks at ~1 Gyr post-burst, similar to the tidal disruption event (TDE) DTD, but QPE hosts exhibit a higher fraction of large burst mass fractions, suggesting large ~1-Gyr-old star formation bursts may preferentially produce the extreme mass ratio inspirals (EMRIs) that drive QPEs.
AI.motivation: QPEs are linked to TDEs and are overrepresented in post-starburst galaxies, yet the physical origin of QPEs and the mechanism driving this overrepresentation remain unknown. Constructing the QPE DTD can constrain the formation channels and mechanisms that influence the QPE rate.
AI.method: The authors compile a catalog of 10 QPE host galaxies with optical spectra, model their stellar populations using the Bagpipes spectral fitting code, and extract the age of the most recent star formation burst to construct the QPE delay time distribution, comparing it to a control sample and TDE host galaxies.
AI.result: The QPE rate rises with post-burst age, peaking at ~1 Gyr relative to a control sample, mirroring the observational TDE DTD, though a flat burst-age distribution cannot be excluded. QPE host galaxies exhibit a higher fraction of >1% burst mass fractions than either TDE hosts or control galaxies.
AI.conclusion: If QPEs primarily form via extreme mass ratio inspirals, such EMRIs may be more readily produced by large, ~1-Gyr-old bursts of star formation, providing a plausible channel linking QPEs to their post-starburst host galaxy environment.

title: CHANG-ES XL: Magnetic Field Structures in the Disk and Halo of NGC 891
comment: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: We present new Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array S-band (2-4 GHz) observations of the edge-on spiral galaxy NGC 891, complemented by C-band data, to investigate the structure of its radio continuum halo. Using rotation measure synthesis we detected an extended polarized halo, with most spatially extended polarized emission confined to Faraday depths within +/- 150 rad m-2. We identified a localized region in the north-east side of the galaxy that shows an enhancement in polarized intensity (not in percentage polarization). By combining the radio data with H-alpha and diffuse X-ray maps, we discuss a possible origin for this structure: a superbubble powered by clustered supernovae. Across the disk and halo, the percentage polarization decreases toward the midplane but shows a mild wavelength dependence, despite the edge-on orientation of NGC 891. This behavior implies that the depolarization cannot be dominated by small-scale Faraday rotation within the disk. Instead, it is possible that most of the observed polarized emission arises on the Earth-facing side of the galaxy. Our peak rotation measure (RM) map shows a smooth transition along the major axis, consistent with a large scale axisymmetric magnetic field. Using H-alpha and UV data, we analyzed the distribution of H II regions and found that they are parts of different spiral arms. We also identified a faint, isolated H II region at a galactocentric radius of 16.9 kpc, with both H-alpha and far-UV counterparts, indicating star formation outside the thin disk.

AI.tldr: New VLA S-band and C-band observations of the edge-on spiral galaxy NGC 891 reveal an extended polarized radio halo with Faraday depths within ±150 rad m⁻², including a localized polarized intensity enhancement in the north-east possibly powered by a superbubble from clustered supernovae. The percentage polarization decreases toward the midplane with mild wavelength dependence, suggesting depolarization is not dominated by small-scale Faraday rotation in the disk and that most polarized emission arises on the Earth-facing side. The rotation measure map shows a smooth transition along the major axis consistent with a large-scale axisymmetric magnetic field, and H-alpha/UV data identify H II regions in different spiral arms plus a faint isolated H II region at 16.9 kpc indicating star formation outside the thin disk.
AI.motivation: To investigate the detailed magnetic field structure and radio continuum halo properties of NGC 891, a prototypical edge-on spiral galaxy, using broadband polarimetric observations to constrain the origin of polarized emission, depolarization mechanisms, and magnetic field geometry.
AI.method: New VLA S-band (2-4 GHz) observations complemented by C-band data, analyzed via rotation measure synthesis to map the polarized halo. Radio data are combined with H-alpha and diffuse X-ray maps to interpret localized structures, and with UV data to analyze H II region distributions.
AI.result: An extended polarized halo is detected with most emission at Faraday depths within ±150 rad m⁻². A localized polarized intensity enhancement (not in percentage polarization) in the north-east is identified as a possible superbubble powered by clustered supernovae. Percentage polarization decreases toward the midplane with mild wavelength dependence, implying depolarization is not dominated by small-scale Faraday rotation in the disk. The RM map shows a smooth transition along the major axis, consistent with an axisymmetric magnetic field. H II regions are distributed across different spiral arms, with an isolated region at 16.9 kpc indicating star formation outside the thin disk.
AI.conclusion: The polarized halo of NGC 891 likely arises predominantly on the Earth-facing side of the galaxy, with depolarization not driven by disk-internal small-scale Faraday rotation. The magnetic field has an axisymmetric large-scale structure. The findings also reveal star formation occurring beyond the thin disk of the galaxy.

title: From Cluster Cores to the Low-Density Field: Strong Environmental Quenching of Galaxy Star Formation at Low Redshift
summary: We investigate how galaxy star formation activity depends on environment using a sample of 81,647 SDSS galaxies selected over $0.03\leq z\leq0.075$ and $9.7\leq\log_{10}(M_\star/h^{-2}M_\odot)\leq11.0$, including 18,426 members from 572 clusters in the \texttt{GalWCat19} catalog. We characterize environment in two complementary ways: (1) nearest-neighbor density for the full sample, and (2) clustercentric radius and host halo mass for \texttt{GalWCat19}. The sSFR distribution remains bimodal across all environments, with distinct quenched and star-forming components. As local density increases, the quenched component becomes more prominent, while the characteristic sSFR of the star-forming component decreases by approximately $0.29$--$0.35$ dex from the lowest- to highest-density classes. Within clusters, the quenched fraction decreases with increasing projected clustercentric radius, while the star-forming peak shifts by approximately $0.42$ dex toward lower sSFR from the outskirts to the inner cluster region. This extends the picture from previous studies, in which environmental trends are primarily associated with changes in the quenched fraction, by showing that galaxies remaining in the star-forming population also exhibit systematically suppressed sSFR in denser environments. The dependence on host halo mass is weaker and is most apparent among lower-stellar-mass galaxies in the inner cluster regions. By measuring the environmental quenching efficiency at fixed stellar mass, we find excess quenching in cluster environments beyond that expected from stellar-mass quenching alone. These results show that environment is associated not only with an increased probability of quenching, but also with suppressed star formation among galaxies that remain star forming, with local density and clustercentric radius showing the strongest associations.

AI.tldr: Using 81,647 SDSS galaxies (18,426 in 572 clusters from GalWCat19), the authors show that the sSFR distribution remains bimodal across all environments, but denser environments both increase the quenched fraction and systematically suppress sSFR in star-forming galaxies by ~0.29-0.42 dex, with local density and clustercentric radius showing the strongest effects while host halo mass matters mainly for low-mass galaxies in cluster cores.
AI.motivation: To understand how galaxy star formation depends on environment, extending previous work that mainly attributed environmental trends to changes in the quenched fraction, by testing whether the star-forming population itself is also suppressed in denser environments.
AI.method: Analyzed 81,647 SDSS galaxies at 0.03≤z≤0.075 and stellar masses 9.7-11.0 dex. Environment characterized two ways: (1) nearest-neighbor local density for the full sample, and (2) clustercentric radius and host halo mass using the GalWCat19 cluster catalog. Examined the sSFR bimodality, quenched fractions, star-forming peak shifts, and environmental quenching efficiency at fixed stellar mass.
AI.result: The sSFR distribution stays bimodal in all environments. The quenched component grows with density while the star-forming peak shifts down by ~0.29-0.35 dex from low to high density. In clusters, quenched fraction decreases outward while the star-forming peak shifts ~0.42 dex lower toward cluster centers. Host halo mass dependence is weaker and strongest for low-mass galaxies in cluster cores. Environmental quenching exceeds stellar-mass quenching alone in clusters.
AI.conclusion: Environment not only raises the probability of quenching but also suppresses star formation in galaxies that remain star-forming, with local density and clustercentric radius being the strongest environmental drivers.
